とどく はず の こづつみ — The parcel that should have arrived

You say what “should” be true by all the signs (～はず だ), what “can’t be” (～はず が ない), what “was supposed to” happen (～はず だった) and “no wonder” (どうりで ～はず だ); in December, when the parcels from Japan are late and the due date is getting close.
it can’t be that…, there’s no way…
was supposed to… (but it didn’t happen)
to take care of (something belonging to someone else)
The parcel should have arrived yesterday.
I was home the whole time, so there’s no way it arrived.
The plane was supposed to land at six.
The due date should be January 15.
It was delayed by the snow? No wonder you were so late.
To form ～はず だ with verbs (present, past, negative), い and な adjectives and nouns (の はず).
To say “it can’t be” with ～はず が ない / ～はず は ない and tell it apart from ～ない はず だ.
To tell what was supposed to happen and didn’t: ～はず だった / ～はず でした.
To use どうりで ～はず だ (“no wonder…”) and to tell はず apart from つもり, よてい and でしょう.

A Saturday morning, a few days before Christmas. Mrs Suzuki and Mrs Fumiko left a few days ago. Two weeks ago Haruka sent a parcel for the baby from Hiroshima, and Yuki sent one from Tokyo. Ana, who is 37 weeks pregnant, is checking the parcel tracking on her phone. Doina speaks Spanish with Ana; her lines are given in Japanese.
Yesterday? But you were home all day.
Yes, I was here the whole time. So there’s no way it arrived. The doorbell didn’t ring either.
Strange. Maybe the courier made a mistake?
Haruka says: “I sent it two weeks ago, so it should have arrived by now.”
Then it must be somewhere. …Hang on, isn’t the doorbell broken?
No way! I changed the battery last month. It can’t have broken.
(Pressing the doorbell from outside) …Huh! It doesn’t ring.
(From the stairs) Ana! Yesterday I took in your parcel. From Japan!
The courier rang, nobody answered, so he left it with me.
So the doorbell was broken. No wonder nobody came.
Mrs Doina, thank you so much! …Oh, there’s a letter from Sakura inside. It says: “The socks are finally done.”
Those socks? The ones she was supposed to be knitting with Haruka…?
(Taking out the socks) Pink socks! …Look, one is a bit bigger.
(Laughing) It’s her first time knitting, there’s no way they’d come out the same size. But that’s amazing.
From Haruka, a bib and a CD of lullabies. “Listen to it when the baby won’t stop crying.”
When was the due date again?
It should be January 15. There isn’t even a month left.
And Yuki’s parcel? She said it should arrive by the 20th.
Not yet. But Yuki sent it properly, there’s no way it got lost.
And Mrs Fumiko’s sweets haven’t come yet, right?
Mrs Fumiko should still be in Madrid, so the sweets from Kyoto should come after New Year.
We’ll ask Mr Petre to fix the doorbell. He should be able to fix it quickly.
“~hazu da” = should…; “~hazu ga nai” = there’s no way…
either, also; “hitotsuki mo” = not even a month
already; “mō hitotsuki mo arimasen” = there isn’t even a month left
“naoshite moraimashō” = let’s ask him to fix it
ha-zu: a voiced “z” as in “zoo”, and the final “u” is almost silent: “haz”. Don’t mix it up with はし (chopsticks) or はこ (box).
ko-zu-tsu-mi: づ is read exactly like ず (“zu”). It appears when つ attaches to another word: こ + つつみ → こづつみ (small package).
doo-ri-de: a long “dō”, then “ri” with the Japanese r (a light tap, between r and l). You say it in an “aha!” tone, when you discover the cause.

はず expresses a LOGICAL expectation, based on information: “from what I know, it must be so”. Haruka sent the parcel two weeks ago → もう ついて いる はず です (it should have arrived by now). はず is a noun, so it connects like a noun.
It should be cold in Kyoto.
The form ～て いる はず shows a state that should already be the case: マドリード に いる はず だ (she should be in Madrid), もう ついて いる はず だ (it should have arrived).

In English we say “should” or “must have”: “he left at 8, he must have arrived by now”. That’s exactly はず: a conclusion from facts, not a wish and not an obligation. For obligation (you have to do it) Japanese uses something else: ～なければ ならない (ch. 15).
2. ～はず が ない: “there’s no way…”
With はず が ない (or はず は ない, a little softer) you say that something is IMPOSSIBLE by your logic: “no way”. Ana was home all day → とどいた はず が ない (there’s no way it arrived).
I expect him not to come
it’s not possible that he’ll come
I changed the battery. It can’t have broken.
It’s her first time knitting, there’s no way they’d come out the same size.
She sent it properly, there’s no way it got lost.

Reality can prove はず が ない wrong too! Mihai and Ana were sure the doorbell couldn’t break, but it was broken. You could say, using ほど from ch. 39: 「はず が ない」 と いう ひと ほど まちがえる (the people who say “it can’t be” are the ones most often wrong).
In the past, はず だった / はず でした tells what was expected to happen but didn’t (or happened differently). It’s very often followed by けど / が.
The plane was supposed to land at six, but it was an hour late.
The parcel was supposed to arrive by the 20th, but it still hasn’t come.
I thought I’d fixed the doorbell… (but no). (You’ll learn のに in ch. 44.)
English does the same with “was supposed to”: “she was supposed to come at six” already hints that she didn’t. Japanese はず だった has the same nuance of a disappointed expectation.
4. どうりで ～はず だ: “no wonder…”
When you find out the CAUSE of something that puzzled you, you say どうりで (or なるほど) + ～はず だ. Here はず is no longer a guess, but “aha, now it makes sense!”.
That’s why you were so late.
That’s why she’s so good at it.
The order is the reverse of a guess: first the fact you discovered, then どうりで + what had puzzled you + はず だ. Without どうりで, the sentence would be a simple guess: さむい はず だ = “it should be cold”.
5. はず, つもり, よてい, でしょう: four kinds of “going to…”
They all concern the future or things you don’t know for sure, but each from a different angle. The most common mistake: はず for YOUR OWN intentions.
I intend to go to Japan.
Carmen is due to come on the 23rd.
He should have reached the airport by now.

✗ わたし は らいねん にほん へ いく はず です. You can’t “draw conclusions” about your own decision. You say いく つもり です (intention) or いく よてい です (plan). Exception: when it doesn’t depend on you, はず works: しごと で いく はず です (because of work, I’m supposed to go).
Think of はず as a calculation: “sent on the 10th + takes 10 days = it should arrive on the 20th”. If you can show the calculation, use はず.
“The parcel should have arrived by now.”
“I was home all day, there’s no way it arrived.”

“The plane was supposed to land at six (but it was late).”
The doorbell was broken. “No wonder nobody came.”

サクラ の てがみ — Sakura’s letter
In the parcel there was also a letter from Sakura, written in pencil, with a drawing of socks in the corner.
Big sister Ana, big brother Mihai, how are you?
The socks are finally done! I learned from Mom and it took me a month.
One is a bit bigger. But the baby’s feet are small too, so they should grow quickly.
Mom said “it should arrive in two weeks”. So it should arrive by Christmas.
The baby should be born in January, right? I practise a lullaby on the piano every day.
There’s no way the baby will forget me. After all, I’m the big sister! Sakura

ゆき と こづつみ — The snow and the parcel
A week before Christmas, Ana taught her last class before the birth at the Spanish school.
After the class, the students gave her a big card.
On the card was a drawing by Andrei: a house with three windows, and at one of the windows there was a tiny baby.
Ana hugged the card to her chest: “Build this house for real one day.”
“Andrei is sure to become a good architect”, Mr Ion said with a laugh.
Cristina, who is a nurse, said with a serious face: “Teacher, babies sometimes come earlier than the due date.”
“Don’t worry. The date is the 15th, so there should still be more than three weeks”, Ana answered.
Cristina wrote her phone number on a slip of paper and gave it to Ana. “If anything happens, call me, even in the middle of the night.”
Mr Ion said too, laughing again: “My grandchildren in Valencia were also born earlier than the due date.”
That evening an email came from Yuki.
“Ana, I sent the parcel on the 10th. It should arrive by the 20th. If it doesn’t, go and scold the post office!”
But the 20th passed, and Yuki’s parcel still didn’t come.
When she checked online, it said: “Being inspected at customs”.
“Customs? There shouldn’t be anything strange inside…” Ana looked at her phone anxiously.
Mihai laughed: “Knowing Yuki, there must be a book inside. There’s no way they’d hold it up for a book. It’ll come soon.”
When Ana wrote to her, Yuki answered right away: “That’s strange. It should have arrived by now… I really will scold the post office!”
The 23rd was the day Carmen was coming from Madrid.
The plane was supposed to land at six. In the afternoon, Mihai went straight from the hospital to the airport to meet her.
Ana waited at home, because her doctor husband had told her: “In cold like this, no airport for you.”
Seven o’clock passed, eight o’clock passed, and the two of them still weren’t back.
“They should have arrived by now…” Ana kept looking out of the window. Outside, a fine snow was falling.
At half past eight the door finally opened and Carmen came in. “Because of the snow, the plane was a whole hour late!”
“No wonder you were so late”, Ana said with a sigh of relief.
Without even taking off her coat, Carmen hugged Ana. Then she looked at her belly and her eyes went wide.
“Goodness, how big it’s got! The 15th? It must be earlier. You were born ten days before your due date too.”
Ana and Mihai looked at each other in silence.
One of the suitcases was full almost entirely of baby clothes. “There’s no way she’ll wear all that!”, said Ana, and Carmen answered: “Babies grow fast.”
In the other suitcase there was jamón and turrón.
That night Ana couldn’t fall asleep for a long time. Carmen’s words kept going round in her head: “It must be earlier.”
On the morning of Christmas Eve the doorbell rang. It was the doorbell Mr Petre had fixed the day before.
Apparently it wasn’t the battery: a wire inside had broken.
When they opened the door, the courier was standing there with a slightly squashed box. It was covered in Japanese stamps.
“It’s from Yuki!” Mihai carried the box to the table.
Inside there was a picture book and a pair of tiny white tabi.
The book was an old Spanish picture book translated into Japanese. On the last page it said: “Edited by Yuki”.
There was a card too: “This is the first book I’ve edited. Please read it to the baby in three languages: Spanish, Romanian and Japanese.”
“See, it was a book. I told you there was no way they’d hold it up”, Mihai said proudly.
“But it was supposed to arrive by the 20th”, Ana laughed. “Same as the doorbell. You can’t really count on “should”.”
That evening Elena came too, and they all had Christmas dinner together.
After dinner, Ana opened the book and tried reading it in Japanese.
Mihai read the same page in Romanian, and Carmen in Spanish.
The two grandmothers hardly share a language. But when the talk turns to cooking, strangely enough, they seem to understand each other perfectly.
Elena beamed: “This child will speak three languages. She must be much cleverer than us.”
Inside the belly, the baby moved. Carmen and Elena cried out together: “She answered!”
When Ana sent Yuki a photo of the book, Yuki replied: “It made it in time for Christmas! Right on schedule!”
Late at night, after everyone had gone to bed, Ana stopped in front of the calendar. There was a red circle on January 15.
“Three more weeks until the due date”, Mihai said from behind her.
“But the baby shouldn’t be able to read a calendar”, said Ana, and Mihai laughed too.
“True. So she can come any time, the hospital bag is already ready by the door.”
Ana put on Haruka’s CD. A gentle lullaby filled the quiet room.
“By the time she’s born, I should be able to sing this song too”, Mihai said softly.
Ana laughed: “With that voice, the baby should fall asleep right away.”
Outside the window, the snow settled quietly.

“~koto mo arimasu” = it sometimes happens; “no koto da kara” = knowing (someone)
“haitte iru” = is inside; “haitte kimashita” = came in
to get held up, to get caught
“mukae ni iku” = to go and meet someone
“tsuite iru” = has arrived; “tsuite imasu” = is on (there)
“yonde agete kudasai” = please read to her; “yonde mimashita” = tried reading
“ate ni naranai” = can’t be counted on
“nikoniko suru” = to beam, to smile broadly
“okotte okimasu” = I’ll scold them (so it’s done)
